subChunks.title: Joining Three or More Tables
subChunks.hookHtml: Real queries often span three or more tables. You chain joins the same way you chain two — each join adds one more table to the result set.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Chaining joins

SELECT a.name, m.name AS mentor, q.title AS quest
FROM   apprentices AS a
INNER JOIN mentors         AS m  ON a.mentor_id = m.id
INNER JOIN quest_completions AS qc ON qc.apprentice_id = a.id
INNER JOIN quests           AS q  ON qc.quest_id = q.id;

Each JOIN adds a table. The ON clause links it to any previously joined table (usually the most recently added one, but not always).

Mixing join types

-- All apprentices, their optional mentor, and any completed quests:
SELECT a.name, m.name AS mentor, q.title AS quest
FROM   apprentices AS a
LEFT JOIN mentors         AS m  ON a.mentor_id = m.id
LEFT JOIN quest_completions AS qc ON qc.apprentice_id = a.id
LEFT JOIN quests           AS q  ON qc.quest_id = q.id;

Order matters with LEFT JOIN + INNER JOIN

If you LEFT JOIN then INNER JOIN to the result, the INNER JOIN can eliminate rows brought in by the LEFT JOIN. Be explicit about intent.

Filtering after multi-table join

WHERE m.specialty = 'Evocation'
AND   q.difficulty = 'Hard'

storyBeats.text: Four ledgers open on the table: apprentices, mentors, quest completions, quests. The Headmaster wants one report spanning all four.

storyBeats.speaker: Cipher the Archivist
storyBeats.text: You chain joins like links in a chain. Each one adds a table. Alias every table — three tables means three aliases. Keep the ON conditions clear and the WHERE clause separate from the join conditions.

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
🪄 Quest report

Join apprentices → quest_completions → quests. Return the apprentice name, the quest title, and the completion score. Only show rows where the quest difficulty is 'Hard'.
subChunks.guidedPracticeStarterCode:
SELECT a.name, q.title, qc.score
FROM   apprentices      AS a
INNER JOIN quest_completions AS qc ON qc.apprentice_id = a.id
INNER JOIN quests            AS q  ON qc.quest_id = q.id
WHERE q.difficulty = 'Hard';

subChunks.soloPracticeHtml:
🏹 Solo

Add the mentors table to the query. Return apprentice name, their mentor's name aliased as mentor, and the quest title for all hard quests. Use LEFT JOIN for the mentor (some apprentices have none).
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Describe how you chain three table joins together in SQL, and explain what can go wrong when mixing LEFT JOIN and INNER JOIN in the same query.

questions.prompt: When chaining joins, what does each JOIN's ON clause connect?
options: The new table to any already-joined table via a matching column pair
The new table only to the table immediately before it
All tables in the FROM clause simultaneously
The new table to the base table only
questions.answer: The new table to any already-joined table via a matching column pair
questions.explanation: Each JOIN adds a table and its ON clause links it to any already-joined table. Usually this is the immediately preceding table, but you can reference any prior table.

questions.prompt: In a query that LEFT JOINs mentors, then INNER JOINs quest_completions, what happens to apprentices with no mentor and no quest completions?
options: They are excluded — the INNER JOIN on quest_completions eliminates rows with no completions
They appear with NULLs in all joined columns
They appear once for the LEFT JOIN and are excluded by the INNER JOIN separately
questions.answer: They are excluded — the INNER JOIN on quest_completions eliminates rows with no completions
questions.explanation: INNER JOIN eliminates any row that has no match. Even if a LEFT JOIN brought an unmatched row into the intermediate result, a subsequent INNER JOIN can eliminate it if the new table has no match.

questions.prompt: A query joins 4 tables and returns 0 rows on data you know exists. The most likely cause is:
options: A missing or incorrect ON condition causing a Cartesian product or filtering everything
NULL values in the primary key columns
ORDER BY coming before GROUP BY
questions.answer: A missing or incorrect ON condition causing a Cartesian product or filtering everything
questions.explanation: Wrong ON conditions (e.g. a.id = b.id instead of a.mentor_id = b.id) either produce millions of rows (Cartesian) or filter everything out. Systematically check each ON condition against the schema.

questions.prompt: What is the best way to debug a multi-table join that returns unexpected rows?
options: Build the query incrementally — add one join at a time and check the row count after each addition
Run the full query and inspect the final output only
Use EXPLAIN to see which join the engine chose
questions.answer: Build the query incrementally — add one join at a time and check the row count after each addition
questions.explanation: Incremental building isolates exactly which join introduces wrong rows. Adding all joins at once and debugging the combined result is much harder. Each intermediate step should produce an understandable row count.
